title: Maximum Deletions on a String
statement:
You get a string `s` of lowercase English letters and remove it piece by piece. Each operation does one of two things:

- remove all of what is left of `s`, or
- pick a length `i` with `1 <= i <= s.length / 2` such that the first `i` characters of the current `s` are identical to the `i` characters right after them, and remove those first `i` characters.

Keep going until `s` is empty. Return the largest number of operations this can take.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Every operation removes a prefix, so what remains is always a suffix `s[i..]`. That makes the suffix start `i` a complete description of the state: let `dp[i]` be the most operations that can clear `s[i..]`. Removing everything at once always works (one operation), and removing `len` letters is allowed exactly when `s[i..i+len)` equals `s[i+len..i+2·len)`, after which `dp[i + len]` more operations follow. Trying all choices recursively on the actual strings is the brute force; the DP does it in O(n²) once substring equality is O(1).

For that, let `lcp[j]` be the length of the longest common prefix of `s[i..]` and `s[j..]`. Then the two halves match exactly when `lcp[i + len] >= len`. These lengths satisfy `lcp(i, j) = lcp(i + 1, j + 1) + 1` when `s[i] === s[j]` (and `0` otherwise), so each row only needs the row for `i + 1`.

## Approach

1. Turn `s` into `codes`, its character codes, so comparisons are cheap.
2. Walk `i` from the last index down to `0`, so `dp[i + len]` is ready when `dp[i]` needs it.
3. Fill row `i` of the common-prefix table into `lcp` from `lcpNext`, the row for `i + 1`.
4. Start `dp[i] = 1`: deleting the whole suffix.
5. For every `len` with `i + 2·len <= n`, if `lcp[i + len] >= len`, try `dp[i + len] + 1`.
6. Swap the two rows and continue. The answer is `dp[0]`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `s = "abcabcdabc"` (`n = 10`), every suffix starting at `i = 9` down to `1` has no prefix immediately repeated, so `dp[1..9]` are all `1`. At `i = 0`, `len = 1` (`"a"` vs `"b"`) and `len = 2` (`"ab"` vs `"ca"`) fail, but `lcp[3] = 3` because `"abc"` repeats at index 3, so `len = 3` gives `dp[3] + 1 = 2`. Longer lengths fail, and the answer is `dp[0] = 2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²): each `i` fills one row of `lcp` and tries up to `n / 2` lengths.
- Space: O(n): `dp` plus two rows of the common-prefix table instead of the full n×n table.

## Pitfalls

- Greedily deleting the shortest repeat is wrong: in `"aaabaab"` the best plan deletes `"a"`, then `"aab"`, then `"a"`.
- Comparing substrings with `slice` inside the DP makes it O(n³), too slow at 4000 characters. Even the O(n²) loop runs millions of times, so compare character codes (`codes`) rather than one-letter strings.
- A full 4000×4000 table of lengths uses a lot of memory; two rows are enough.
- The final "delete everything" counts as an operation, so `dp[i]` starts at `1`, not `0`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `s` |
| `codes` | character codes of `s`, for fast comparisons |
| `dp[i]` | most operations that can clear the suffix `s[i..]` |
| `lcp[j]` | longest common prefix of `s[i..]` and `s[j..]` |
| `lcpNext[j]` | the same for `s[i + 1..]` and `s[j..]` |
| `i`, `j` | start of the current suffix, start of the suffix compared with it |
| `len` | length of the prefix we try to delete |

narration.3: Work with character codes, which are cheaper to compare than one-letter strings.
narration.4: dp[i] will hold the most operations that can clear the suffix starting at i.
narration.5: lcp holds, for the current i, how far s[i..] and s[j..] agree.
narration.6: lcpNext holds the same lengths for i + 1, which row i is built from.
narration.8: Go from the end so the shorter suffixes are solved first.
narration.9: Fill this row of common-prefix lengths for every later start j.
narration.10: Matching letters extend the match of the next positions by one; a mismatch resets it to zero.
narration.12: Deleting the whole suffix is always possible, so at least one operation.
narration.13: Try every prefix length whose copy still fits after it.
narration.14: Do the first len letters repeat right after themselves?
narration.15: Then delete them and add the best count for the suffix that remains.
narration.18: Reuse the old row's memory for the next i.
narration.20: The whole string is the suffix starting at 0.
